resources.string: Set up and control a Debian 13 server that starts before Android’s first unlock and stays running afterward. Complete the sections from top to bottom once; routine controls and SSH access remain easy to reach.

The new public key is saved in BFU storage. Run Configure Debian 13 systemd + SSH to install it into Debian, then export/import the new private key into your SSH client.

No external shell packages are required. The app includes source-built bootstrap tools for ARMv7, ARM64, and x86_64, verifies pinned Debian metadata and packages, then publishes the completed rootfs to /data/local/debian.

This first stops the standalone Debian supervisor, verifies that no systemd process remains, then permanently deletes exactly /data/local/debian. All Debian packages, users, password hashes, SSH host keys, and in-rootfs configuration will be lost. App DE settings and logs are retained.

This uses the source-built bootstrap runtime bundled for your device ABI, downloads signed Debian 13 Trixie packages, and runs upstream debootstrap as pre-authorized Magisk root. Existing /data/local/debian is never overwritten or upgraded in place. Keep this app open to watch the live log.

After the Trixie rootfs install succeeds, this AFU-only step installs systemd, D-Bus, and OpenSSH. It creates user debian, copies the validated DE public keys, disables password/root login, enables ssh.service on TCP 22, masks Android-host-sensitive units, and writes the BFU-ready marker only after validation.

This temporarily stops a running BFU Debian instance, uses apt inside /data/local/debian, and then starts the configured system again for validation. SSH accepts only the public keys shown above. Keep this app open to watch the live log.

Debian starts automatically during LOCKED_BOOT_COMPLETED after all BFU gates pass. USER_UNLOCKED never stops or restarts it. Start, restart, and status also verify systemd PID 1, D-Bus, ssh.service, and TCP 22; results are persisted in the DE log.
This explicitly asks the Debian container service manager to exit gracefully and stops SSH. Unlock events do not perform this action.
This gracefully exits the verified Debian PID 1, starts a fresh isolated instance, then waits for D-Bus, SSH, and TCP 22 health checks. USER_UNLOCKED never performs this action.

DawnShell checks kernel capabilities at runtime instead of guessing from the version string. Auto modes try the modern backend first and fall back only after a bounded probe fails and temporary probe state is cleaned.

This selection takes effect on the next Debian start or restart. Automatic mode adopts v2 only after a dedicated cgroup2 subtree in a private mount view and cgroup-device BPF attach both succeed. Force v2 disables the known-good v1 fallback and can prevent Debian from booting. Force v1 skips modern isolation and attaches the legacy devices controller to a hierarchy; Android tasks remain outside DawnShell’s delegated child, but this is still a kernel-global controller attachment.
Controls raw USBFS access and optional driver unbinding. This is not complete USB-device isolation because Debian and Android share the same kernel, sysfs, and network namespace.

Policy scope

• Off blocks /dev/bus/usb and USB character major 189, preventing ordinary libusb/raw USBFS access.
• Off does not stop Android from detecting USB hardware. USB topology can remain visible through shared /sys.
• Devices already claimed by Android kernel drivers can expose derived resources to Debian, including /dev/block/sd* storage, USB Ethernet interfaces, ttyUSB/ttyACM serial ports, input, video, or audio nodes. These are not blocked by the raw USBFS policy.
• Sharing exposes raw USBFS while retaining Android drivers. Exclusive passthrough additionally unbinds only interfaces matching the VID:PID list; it is not USB virtualization.
Off: block raw USBFS only; derived devices remain visible (recommended)
Raw USBFS sharing: keep Android drivers
Comma or space separated, for example 0403:6001, 10c4:ea60. At least one entry is required for exclusive mode.
Enter at least one USB VID:PID before enabling exclusive passthrough.
Use four hexadecimal vendor digits, a colon, and four product digits for every USB ID.

DANGER: Use Apply USB sharing policy after changing this setting. A running Debian restarts; a stopped Debian uses it on the next start. The policy also applies to devices attached later. Sharing mode gives Debian raw /dev/bus/usb access while retaining Android drivers. Exclusive passthrough additionally disconnects matching interfaces from Android and tries to restore them when Debian stops; Android input, storage, networking, ADB, or recovery access can disappear, and a crash may require unplugging the device or rebooting. Never select the phone’s internal USB/gadget controller. Never mount one USB storage filesystem from both systems. Docker still requires --device. Kernel drivers and SELinux can deny access.
Unlock Android before applying USB sharing.

DawnShell will save this USB policy. If Debian is running, it will restart so the private mount and device cgroup policy change together. Active SSH sessions will disconnect. A stopped Debian remains stopped and uses the policy on its next start.
USB sharing policy is being applied. Running Debian will restart.
Automatic: native nftables → iptables-nft → legacy → safe host
Automatically use host IPC for Docker run/create

Compatibility option for kernels where private IPC/mqueue fails. Containers share Android and Debian IPC objects, reducing isolation. Apply the Docker policy after changing it. An explicit --ipc option overrides this default; /usr/bin/docker bypasses the wrapper.

DANGER: DawnShell deliberately shares Android’s network namespace for native NIC speed. Every bridge option lets Docker modify Android-global firewall, NAT, forwarding, and routes. It can break Wi-Fi, mobile data, USB Ethernet, VPN/Tailscale, or remote access. Host-only mode disables Docker bridge/firewall management and requires Docker host networking. All managed modes use Docker’s cgroupfs driver inside DawnShell’s private delegated hierarchy; the systemd driver is incompatible with some Android kernels.
Unlock Android before changing Docker networking.

DawnShell will stop Debian if it is running, disable Docker bridge, NAT, forwarding, and firewall management, then restore the previous Debian running state. Containers must use Docker host networking.

This mode can modify Android-global firewall, NAT, forwarding, and routes because Debian shares Android’s network namespace. DawnShell will stop Debian, probe the selected backend, apply the managed Docker configuration, and restore the previous running state.
